# Abstract

Working memory load in humans is readily conveyed through EEG sensor data, which provides the excellent temporal resolution needed for accurate data analysis. We use working memory as defined by the n-back experiment, which correlates working memory demand with the variable n, run in tandem with EEG sensor measurements, which provide the necessary features for our data analysis. We aggregate several datasets into one based on the similarity of their measurement methods, lack of disparate columns, and identical experiment paradigm to create a large dataset capable of supporting machine learning workflows. We conduct exploratory data analysis on this resulting data, extract key pattersn that affect classification, and deploy a decomposition algorithm from the parent study on the data. We deploy a suite of feature-based classifiers to infer working memory demand from this EEG data, comparing model performance to each other and to the performance of models in existing studies. We further verify this performance with the use of several evaluation techniques, most importantly confusion matrices and ROC curves, which provide the necessary insights into real model performance on unseen data. We find that n=0 and n=2 can readily be classified at modest accuracies, with our pipeline overperforming that of the parent study. We find that adjacent n-levels are difficult to classify with the same accuracy due to inconsistencies in their band power patterns. 

# Introduction

Through the review of several previous studies on the study of EEG signals to derive classifications and predictions, EEG has been found to offer rich feature sets to inform many types of inferences. This is a promising concept in the topic of machine learning applied to human cognition, in which one of the main challenges is finding ways to measure human cognition in a manner which produces machine-readable patterns. EEG demonstrates this capacity in existing research through the use of data cleaning, feature extraction and further optimizations for downstream classifiers, which yields compelling accuracy and recall results on several cognitive task classifications.

An important, and intuitive, paradigm of machine learning use in human cognition is the classification of working memory usage, which at face value, offers a continuous unbroken target variable that exhibits deltas in degrees of intensity. These characteristics of working memory are due to its well-studied limitations in humans, which are generally quite thin; the average human can only hold around 4-7 chunks of information in their working memory at a given moment. This makes working memory easily measurable, since subject performance in memory tests degrades predictably. Consequently, machine learning is intuitively applied in this paradigm - since there are clear average boundaries in human working memory, a classifier can distinguish between them, given adequate sensor information.

EEG fulfills this sensing criteria. The measurement method - a cap of electrodes placed on the cranium - measures the amplitude and frequency of electrical impulses traveling across the brain. Because of the speed at which these impulses travel, EEG has excellent temporal resolution; the time it takes for a change in cognition to be registered by the sensors is negligible, making it highly accurate for downstream analysis. There is also a wealth of open-access EEG data available due to the age of the technology, making the construction of a dataset for machine-classified working memory feasible.

Working memory is readily measured through the conduction of the n-back experiment, where a subject must remember a rotating set of numbers and compare them to new stimuli. A given 2-back workflow would look like this:

- The subject is given two numbers to memorize.

- The subject is shown a third number, and must return whether the number matches one number in the set.

- The third number is then appended to the memorized set (and the first number in the set dropped) and the experiment continues.

On average, subject performance heavily drops as n grows, which is consistent with real-world working memory capabilities. In the scope of our research, the n-back experiment will be used as the pivot of our downstream classification. The target variable will be n (the number of backs in the experiment) and the EEG sensor data will provide features for the classifiers.

The questions we would like to answer with this research are the following: - Can machine learning be implemented to classify different levels of working memory demand using EEG sensor data? - Can a comparable model performance be derived from classifying working memory levels, against only classifying the use of working memory entirely?

# Literature Review

Classifying EEG signals with machine learning is an ongoing multi-pronged endeavor in both acquiring the necessary data for analysis, and developing innovative mathematical methods to achieve the best results on the downstream models. We review several data descriptors and research papers, which have brought forth findings on analyzing EEG measurements that not only form the basis of this research, but also provide the necessary data to conduct analysis and train models. The most important of these studies for our findings was the research by Shin et al. on hybridizing EEG and fNIRS data, which saw the use of the n-back experiment for working memory demand and a downstream classification of this experiment using the hybrid dataset, which provided the method for our research and the focus on working memory and the n-back experiment.

Shin et al. provided the basis of our n-back tests as well as a data repository in their data descriptor on hybridizing EEG and fNIRS readings to create a more effective dataset. Their justification for this was the inherent disparity between the two methods; EEG has high temporal resolution (quick response sensing) but low spatial resolution (difficult to pinpoint measurement areas) while fNIRS has the opposite issues. Therefore, creating a dataset that hosts both of these methods can harness their individual strengths and address their weaknesses. Their methods hinged on the experiment paradigm, which involved the simultaneous acquisition of both sets of measurements via customized placement of EEG and fNIRS sensor nodes. Their work proved that the creation of such a hybridized dataset is possible and results in usable data, and also introduced the concept of using this hybrid data to improve classifier performance, compared to only using EEG or fNIRS data alone. While out of scope for our research, this is a potential elaboration on the topic of classifying brain measurements.

To develop a mathematical pipeline that cleans EEG data for enhanced downstream analysis and classification, Yedukondalu et al., the authors of the parent study, developed an innovative workflow that combines aggressive data cleaning steps with several robust algorithms, most notably robust-local mean decomposition. This workflow was applied to the open-access MAT and STEW datasets, which were cleaned and run through R-LMD, feature extraction, and finally classified via ensemble classification. The paper’s goal was to optimize for efficient analysis methods that challenge state-of-the-art classification tools in accuracy, using consistent open-access data that allows for iteration upon former methods. Their accuracy results are promising (97.4% accuracy on MAT, 96.1% on STEW) and pointed us to R-LMD for a potential EEG decomposition method. However, their methods of gathering this accuracy from model performance are flawed due to a cross-validation technique in their pipeline that reveals test data in the training set, endangering memorization by the ensemble models. Their focus on mathematical decomposition is the most invaluable portion of their research to our scope.

Bintay Shafi et al. addresses gaps in existing cognitive load classification methods by intentionally integrating noise and multitasking into their signal, and comparing classification results between a noise-free EEG dataset and a noisy EEG dataset with the same set of participants and tasks. Their goal was to apply existing techniques to a more realistic data collection scenario, effectively “stress-testing” these methods and optimizing for noisy data with new methods. While the nature of their research (multitasking signals) makes their resulting dataset unusable for our purposes, they point us to the COG-BCI dataset in their review of existing data, which provides 0, 1, and 2-back trials which, when combined with the data acquired by Shin et al, yield promising classification results.

For our study, we have revised and modified the implementation undergone by Yedukondalu et al. in training classifiers on EEG data using an in-depth decomposition pipeline. We use differing data sets - COG-BCI and the data obtained from the study by Shin et al., and join these into a large tabular CSV to enable feature-trained downstream model selection. We address data leakage issues in the original parent study by Yedukondalu et al. and provide our own approach to prevent this. We compare the results of our models to those in the parent study and other baselines to get a clearer picture on the limits of feature-based ML on working memory use classification.

# Methodology

The following section discusses our key divergences from the parent study by Yedukondalu et al., tabulates our considerations for how we would implement a given stage in the data science pipeline, and explains, in depth, our final decision on a given task. Then, since the downstream machine learning pipeline differs greatly from that used in the parent study, we simply detail the steps of our work. 

## 1. Data

### Datasets

The datasets used by Yedukondalu et al. were the MAT and STEW EEG datasets, with 36 and 42 participants, respectively. They include the results of multiple cognitive tasks. They are out of scope for this study, because neither of them contain the n-back experiment. The dataset choice represents our first key divergence from the parent study.

```{r}

library(kableExtra)
library(dplyr)

datasets <- data.frame(
  `Dataset` = c('MAT (36 subjects)', 'STEW (42 subjects)', 'iNCog-EEG (40 subjects)', 'Shin 2018 (26 subjects)', 'COG-BCI v4 (29 subjects)'),
  `Source` = c('Yedukondalu et al.', 'Yedukondalu et al.', 'iNCog 2026', 'Shin 2018', 'COG-BCI 2023'),
  `Description` = c('Original parent study dataset. Out of scope due to lack of n-back experiment.', 'Original parent study dataset. Out of scope due to lack of n-back experiment.', 'Multitasking dataset containing n-back task. Left out due to confounding data with other tasks and time.', 'n-back experiment dataset with per-trial behavior. Included in joined dataset.', '4th version of the original COG-BCI n-back dataset that fixed some bugs in participants 17-24 and an electrode name mismatch.'),
  `Decision` = c('Not selected', 'Not selected', 'Not selected', 'Selected', 'Selected')
)

kbl(datasets, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "\\addlinespace",
    caption = "Datasets considered for downstream analysis") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3cm") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "2.6cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "6.6cm") |>
  column_spec(4, width = "2cm")
```

The Shin 2018 n-back dataset and the COG-BCI v4 were chosen for downstream joining and analysis. They both exclusively contain n-back results from their respective studies, with Shin including n-values 0, 2, 3, while COG-BCI v4 includes n-values 0, 1, 2. The shared n-values 0 and 2 will be used for analysis on the first and second research question in the joined dataset, while the individual datasets will be used exclusively for the second research question (classifying levels of working memory load, as opposed to classifying between the presence and non-presence of load).

### Joins

Yedukondalu et al. conducted their data analysis on the MAT and STEW datasets independently, comparing results of similar pipeline procedures once the data was completely processed. We approach the use of our data from an aggregation perspective; by merging Shin 2018 with COG-BCI to create a larger dataset, we facilitate more accurate downstream model performance.

```{r}

joins <- data.frame(
  `Technique` = c('Inner Joins', 'Key Joins'),
  `Description` = c('Union of rows, inner join on channels and on the label domain (eliminating NAs)', 'Key join on subjects shared between studies'),
  `Decision` = c('Selected', 'Not Selected'),
  `Result` = c('26 channels, levels 0-3, 0 and 2 shared by datasets', 'Impossible: no subject appears in both datasets')
)

kbl(joins, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "\\addlinespace",
    caption = "Join methods for aggregated data") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "2.4cm") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "5.6cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "2.2cm") |>
  column_spec(4, width = "4.6cm")
```

Because no subjects were shared across Shin 2018 and COG-BCI, a feature-based inner join was required. This allowed data aggregation while keeping complete rows. n-levels 0 and 2 were shared by both datasets, while for classifying between several n-levels, using the individual datasets was required. 

## 2. Machine Learning

### Validation

The original cross-validation technique used by Yedukondalu et al. was a pooled segments technique, where all subjects were randomly selected from for cross-validation. This technique resulted in data leakage due to each recording in the raw datasets containing one condition, therefore letting the model find labels by simply identifying the recordings in the validation. We resolve this issue by using an alternative cross-validation technique.

```{r}

vals <- data.frame(
  `Technique` = c('10-fold randomized CV', 'Leave-one-subject-out', 'Stratified 10-fold over windows', 'Subject-wise 10-fold', 'Leave-one-dataset-out'),
  `Description` = c('CV used in Yedukondalu study. Susceptible to recording leakage leading to inflated accuracy.', 'Unseen subjects for validation.', 'Taken from iNCog 2026. No scheme for this technique given.', 'CV across subjects. Used as a viability baseline.', 'Cross-dataset check. (Entire datasets unseen)'),
  `Decision` = c('Not Selected', 'Not Selected', 'Not Selected', 'Selected', 'Selected')
)

kbl(vals, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "\\addlinespace",
    caption = "Cross-validation techniques") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3cm") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "6.5cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "2.2cm")
```

Subject-wise 10-fold cross validation was chosen as a viability baseline for downstream classification. Folding across subjects means that the classifier is validated on its performance for a subject when trained on only other people. This also resolves the data leakage issue because it no longer leaks different record types across training data. Leave-one-dataset-out CV is used as a further validation technique to ensure completely unused data for evaluation.

### Train-test-validation splitting

Similar to their cross-validation implementation, Yedukondalu et al. use a technique for train-test splitting that exposes testing data in the training sets. They implement randomized window splitting, which resulted in all 55 subjects in our data leaking across all sets, leading to inflated accuracy in the downstream pipeline. We implement an alternate split method which resolves the data leakage issue. 

```{r}

splits <- data.frame(
  `Method` = c('Whole windows, stratified by dataset', 'Whole blocks, stratified by dataset', 'Whole sessions, stratified by dataset', 'Whole subjects, unstratified', 'Whole subjects, stratified by dataset x Cz interpolation, seed 0'),
  `Description` = c('Split method used in Yedukondalu study. Leads to leakage from all subjects in all sets.', 'All 55 subjects leak across sets.', 'Leaking from 37/55 subjects.', 'No leak, but share of Shin data is unbalanced', 'No leak, balanced data shares'),
  `Decision` = c('Not Selected', 'Not Selected', 'Not Selected', 'Not Selected', 'Selected')
)

kbl(splits, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "\\addlinespace",
    caption = "Data splitting methods") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3.5cm") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "6.25cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "2.2cm")
```

We chose a 70-20-10 split on entire subjects, stratified by the dataset. Splitting on subjects resolves the data leakage issue and results in no subjects appearing in multiple sets, disallowing memorization from the downstream models. Stratifying these selections by dataset allowed an equal share of each set in these splits.

## 3. Downstream implementation

After reproduction of Yedukondalu's pipeline, save for the main changes as discussed, our study diverges sharply from the implementation present in the parent study. We discuss our exploratory data analysis process, findings gained from this analysis, then R-LMD implementation, baseline generation, and downstream feature-based classifier training.

### Exploratory Data Analysis

An analysis was run targeting the mean spectrum by level during a given n-back task on the training data, where the axes of the graph depict band power over a spectrum (with alpha bands highlighted, as they show an important signal), and each n-level is given its own line on the graph. 

![Alpha wave power drops as n rises](figures/eda_psd.png){width=65% fig-align='center'}

The main finding from this analysis is in the alpha peaks at band frequency around 10 Hz; as n rises, alpha power tends to drop lower. In EEG, band power in the alpha frequency correlates to brain relaxation and calm, which tends to decrease as cognitive load in any capacity increases. Alpha power dropping relative to n rising establishes a direct correlation between n and cognitive load, which is further correlated to working memory load with further analysis. 

The correlation between n to working memory demand is further stated with a topomap that visualizes the change in band power across the cranium as n rises from 0 to the top level (3 in Shin 2018, 2 in COG-BCI).

![Mean increase in theta power, mean decrease in alpha power](figures/eda_topomap.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}

In the topomap visual, a red region indicates a mean increase in power, while a blue region indicates a mean decrease in power. Two main observations can be made from this visualization: 

- Alpha band power follows the same trend seen in the previous visual, and decreases as n rises on average.

- Theta band power, which is associated directly with working memory demand, increases as n rises, supporting the correlation between n and working memory usage. 

While correlating n directly with working memory load establishes a relationship, it does not translate completely to impressive downstream model performance. This uncertainty is demonstrated by a further analysis on mean power across all subjects in different n levels. 

![Disparate patterns across datasets in band power level](figures/eda_roi.png){fig-align="center"}

In the figure, each subject of the experiment gets one gray line, and the mean of their power levels across n levels and alpha/theta waves. The key takeaway is a chance of model confusion; in Shin 2018, alpha waves drop from 0-2, then plateau from 2-3, and in COG-BCI waves plateau from 0-1, then drop from 1-2. The disparity in these means leads to inconsistent data for downstream models, which could explain poor model performance in any capacity. 

To verify the most important features to downstream classification, we conducted principal component analysis. Analysis revealed one central component to the entire dataset; alpha band power across and within subjects. The figure generated has the following components: 

- Top left, middle: PC1 z-scored across and within subjects, respectively. 

- Top right: What exactly contributes to PC variance. 

- Bottom left: total # of PCs required to account for 90% variance, across and within. 

- Bottom middle, right: PC1's loading. Alpha power is primarily selected, so this is arguably interchangeable with it.

![Collected PCA results](figures/eda_pca.png){width=75% fig-align="center"}

The main takeaways from PCA were that alpha band power largely accounts for most variance across the data, but is closely related to subject identity. The top left depictions of PC1 z-scoring show completely overlapped alpha power across subjects, while within subjects there is a clear decrease in alpha band power in 2-back. This correlates to the alpha decrease seen in earlier analysis as n increases. The top right depiction reveals the main driver behind variance in data: the subjects identity, which outweighs all other shares of variance by several degrees. Once subjects are normalized, PC1 carries the most load signal. 

### R-LMD Implementation

Robust Local Mean Decomposition is the main method from the parent study that we sought to replicate in this study. It is an adaptive feature extractor that operates on the core idea of extracting further signal from fixed EEG frequency bands. 

Traditional EEG measures and classifies on pre-selected waves, in this case alpha, beta, and theta bands, which are distributed across the entire measured brainwave spectrum. R-LMD allows these frequencies to instead split themselves, classifying themselves into levels and amplitudes of wave oscillations. The deecomposition uses the following procedure: 

1. Find local maxima and minima of the signal

2. Build local mean, local amplitude (midpoint between max/minima, half the distance, smoothed into curves with moving average)

3. "Sifting" - Flattening the signal by subtracing local mean, dividing by local amplitude, and repeating

4. Find fastest oscillation in the signal, form PF1

5. Find next fastest oscillations after subtracting PF1, repeat until applying residuals to PF5

These five outputs are applied to several features: 

- Skewness (SN): The asymmetry of the amplitude distribution
- Kurtosis (KT): How spiky or heavy-tailed the aplitude is
- Mean power spectral density (PSD): How much power the mode has
- Fuzzy entropy (FE): How irregular the waveform is
- Rényi entropy (RE): How spread out the waveforms values are
- Differential entropy (DE): Log power

In our implementation of R-LMD, an analysis foumd that generally, only mode 1 carried load signal. This is due to our data being filtered from 1-40Hz, which is picked up mainly by mode 1.

![Mode 1 is largely the only mode that contains signal in R-LMD output](figures/eda_anova.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

The result of this analysis is that R-LMD effectively measures what raw alpha and beta band power already measure, but with much higher computational overhead. In the parent study, Yedukondalu et al. argued that an adaptive decomposition like R-LMD captures signal that fixed bands miss, but their presented results came mainly from leaked data, as discussed earlier in this section. In our study, R-LMD was run on all signals from the joined dataset, and its features were then given to several downstream classifiers.

### Baselines

Four baseline classifiers were trained to provide a benchmark for downstream model evaluation. They cover standard feature-based classifiers, a deep neural network designed specifically for EEG, and two approaches to reproducing the pipeline of the parent study; one that fully reproduces the work, including the leaky validation methods, and one that corrects the data leakage to return model scoring that more accurately evaluates the downstream classifier. 

1. **Logistic Regression:** Trained on band power with 260 features. CV accuracy on joined sets was 71.07%. Test accuracy came out to 68.8%; test AUC came out to 75.76.

2. **EEGNet:** The EEG-specific deep neural network (DNN). Trained on the EEG signal itself. No cross-validation was applied due to lack of tabular features. Test accuracy came out to 69.09%; test AUC came out to 75.84.

3. **Yedukondalu ensemble (leaky):** The original parent studys' decomposition pipeline, plus their ensemble classification, with the leaky CV methods retained. CV accuracy on joined sets was 88.17%. Test accuracy came out to 60.55%; test AUC came out to 66.27.

4. **Yedukondalu ensemble (corrected):** The same pipeline as above, but with a corrected CV method that eliminates data leakage for a real score. CV accuracy on joined sets was 59.41%. Test accuracy came out to 61.86%; test AUC came out to 68.98.

```{r}

baselines <- data.frame(
  `Model` = c('Logistic regression', 'EEGNet', 'Yedukondalu (L)', 'Yedukondalu (C)'),
  `CV` = c('Subject-wise 5-fold', 'NA', 'Window-wise 10-fold', 'Subject-wise 10-fold'),
  `CV_Accuracy` = c('71.07%', 'NA', '88.17%', '59.41%'),
  `Test_Accuracy` = c('68.8%', '69.09%', '60.55%', '61.86%'),
  `AUC` = c('75.76', '75.84', '66.27', '68.98')
)

kbl(baselines, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "\\addlinespace",
    caption = "Baseline classifiers") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "3cm") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "4cm") |>
  column_spec(3, width = "2cm") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "2cm") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "2cm")
```

### Model Training

Five classifiers were trained on three separate datasets: the joined Shin 2018/COG-BCI data, and the individual datasets themselves. Results from the joined dataset were used for RQ1 ("Can working memory load be classified?") while the individual datasets were for RQ2 ("Can comparable results be achieved distinguishing between working memory demand levels?") All models were given tuned inputs and hyperparameters were tuned based on appropriate metrics. Once all models were optimized, a final classifier was created as a soft vote between chosen models that performed satisfactorily. A variety of trees and perceptron-based classifiers were selected to cover several methods of machine learning for this final soft vote. 

1. **Support Vector Machine:** Trained on band power features, and normalized via within-subject z-scoring. Tuned via subject-wise 5-fold CV and balanced accuracy.

2. **Multilayer Perceptron:** Same training, normalization, and tuning parameters as SVM.

3. **Random Forest:** Trained on band power features and R-LMD features (1,040 features overall). Normalized via within-subject z-scoring, and tuned with subject-wise 5-fold CV.

4. **XGBoost:** Same trainng, normalization, and tuning parameters as RF.

5. **Riemannian Tangent Space:** Trained on theta/alpha/beta covariances (975 features overall). Normalized by re-centering each subject to its own Riemannian mean. Tuned via subject-wise 5-fold CV. RTS transforms EEG windows to invertible covariance matrices, which reintroduces covariance information to the signal.

6. **Soft Vote:** The consensus of the best-performing models on a given dataset. It uses the mean probability of the candidates that pass a validation gate, which enforces the following rules per candidate model: 

   - every class's recall must be above 1/k;
  
   - every class's precision must be above that class's prevalence;

   - the lower 95% bound of its AUC, bootstrapped over validation subjects, must remain over 50. 

   The soft vote only excluded models on COG-BCI; RF and RTS did not pass the gate. On the joined dataset and Shin 2018, all models were included in the soft vote. 

Models were separately trained and validated on the three separate datasets mentioned before: The joined dataset, Shin 2018, and COG-BCI. The joined dataset was used to train the classifiers on a binary classification between n=0 and n=2, which were the only two n-levels shared by Shin 2018 and COG-BCI. Then, the models were trained on the individual datasets to classify between several n-levels; 0, 2, 3 for Shin 2018, and 0, 1, 2 for COG-BCI. The research questions direcltly align to these training cycles - results on the joined dataset correlate to RQ1, while results on the individual datasets correlate to RQ2. 

### Model Evaluation

All baselines and tested classifiers were evaluated with the following metrics: 

- **Cross-validation:** Subject-wise 5-fold for all models except the Yedukondalu leaky and corrected baselines, which used window-wise 10-fold and subject-wise 10-fold, respectively. 

- **Validation balanced accuracy:** Decided which models to pick for vote gating and testing. 

- **Test accuracy and balanced accuracy:** Logged in conjunction with several granular metrics. 

  - Low balanced accuracy

  - High balanced accuracy

- **Test kappa:** The difference between the model's performance and chance

- **Test AUC:** Derived from analysis of the ROC curves

- **Smoothed 20-second metrics:** Since 4-second windows are noisy, smoothing mean decisions over 20 seconds results in more consistent evaluation
  
  - Smoothed balanced accuracy

  - Smoothed AUC

- **Diffs vs EEGNet and Yedukondalu:** Whether the model beats these baselines, segmented to high, low, and median, on EEGNet, Yedukondalu (L) and Yedukondalu (C)

The best candidate was determined to be the model with the best validation balanced accuracy. Test data was scored once per model.

# Results

Every tested classifier outperformed the leakage-corrected Yedukondalu pipeline on all three datasets. This is not limited to only the trees and perceptrons; logistic regression and EEGNet also outperform the corrected pipeline on all tasks, making it the weakest model across the entire analysis. Between the tested models, none of them significantly outperform logistic regression or EEGNet on the data, with the exception of Shin 2018, where EEGNet only has 18 training subjects. 

![Test performance of all downstream classifiers.](figures/eval_summary.png){width=80%, fig-align="center"}

No model outperforms all others by more than 1-3 points, so it is difficult to pin an exact best candidate, although by the validation balanced accuracy rule, three technical best candidates were identified. The best model candidate for the joined datasets was the soft vote between 5 models, which had a balanced validation accuracy of 72.16%, compared to the next highest BVA of 70.79%. The best model candidate for Shin 2018 was Random Forest, which had a BVA of 54.05%, compared to the next highest BVA of 53.81%. The best model candidate for COG-BCI was XGBoost, which had a BVA of 48.89%, compared to the next highest BVA of 47.76%. 

The soft vote does not exhibit an outright overperformance compared to the other classifiers, but does reliably show up in the upper quartile of results, suggesting that the vote helps accuracy to a small degree and does not negatively affect performance in our pipeline. Potentially, a soft vote with more stringent gate criteria could have stronger performance, at the cost of less reliable results due to fewer votes from competent models. 

The 20-second causal smoothing method adds 2-3 points to balanced accuracy on average, likely due to it naturally reducing the effects that a noisy 4-second window has on overall model performance. The performance gains are consistent across models, but are modest, and should be interpreted as an example of the effects of noise smoothing, rather than a procedure for instantaneous improved model performance. 

Confusion matrices were plotted for all models for the joined dataset, Shin 2018, and COG-BCI. These matrices demonstrate a clear distinction between model performance in the joined dataset (classifying between n=0 and n=2) and in the individual datasets (classifying between several n levels) and provide plausible answers to both research questions. 

![Confusion matrix for the joined dataset.](figures/eval_confusion_bin.png){width=75% fig-align="center"}

![Confusion matrix for Shin 2018.](figures/eval_confusion_shin3.png){width=75% fig-align="center"}

![Confusion matrix for COG-BCI.](figures/eval_confusion_cog3.png){width=75% fig-align="center"}

The main takeaways from these matrices are that working memory load (n) **can** be classified from EEG sensor data (RQ1) but is more difficult to classify with the same performance between multiple different load levels (RQ2). The reason for this disparity is due to the patterns exhibited in Fig. 3 during the exploratory data analysis. Band power in the individual datasets is inconsistent between each other and within themselves, and does not linearly correlate to n-level, and in some cases, does not correlate at all. Shin 2018 theta band power rises from n=0 to n=2, but plateaus afterward, which creates no meaningful signal for a classifier. However, because of the overall consistent trend from n=0 to n!=0 as depicted in Fig. 2, classifying between the use of working memory and the disuse of working memory is quite feasible. 

ROC curves were plotted to show model likelihood to classify new subjects correctly as they are shown them. In general, the soft vote sits at the top of these ROC curves, but no model heavily outperforms each other or the baselines, as can be seen by the compact clustering of their curves. This is with the sole exception of the Yedukondalu leakage-corrected pipeline, which severely underperforms all baselines and all tested models. 

![ROC curves of all baselines and tested models.](figures/eval_roc.png){width=80% fig-align="center"}

The underperformance of the parent study's downstream model underscores the skew of their results due to data leakage in the original study. This disparity was also plotted after model evaluation, where all classifiers present in their ensemble were evaluated on both the leaky and corrected pipeline results. 

![Performance disparity between leaky and corrected Yedukondalu models.](figures/eval_leakage.png){width=80% fig-align="center"}

Due to the leaky cross-validation present in the original Yedukondalu pipeline, CV performance estimates are heavily inflated over the test results by over 20 points in some cases. When corrected for this data leakage by using subject-wise CV and eliminating the data leakage in data splitting, model performance stats decrease drastically, leading to this pipeline scoring the lowest of all tested classifiers. We hypotheize two issues that may cost this pipeline accuracy: 

- The pipeline z-scores across pooled subjects, so any subject differences are left in the features

- BAO, an optimization algorithm implemented in their pipeline, keeps under 20% of the 780 R-LMD features, which leads to very little data that can carry over to new subjects.

The overall evaluation displays promising model performance across all implementations in our pipeline, and potential improvements to be made to the pipeline used in the Yedukondalu study. 

## Limitations

This study exhibits several limitations of current work, for which several solutions are proposed in the Future Work section. 

1. **The sizes of the validation and test sets are too small:** The test set holds 11 subjects for the joined dataset, and the validation set holds 6 subjects. This limits the precision of model selection, evaluation, and ranking because test and validation results are extremely volatile. While our models clearly outperform the Yedukondalu baseline, it is unclear which model objectively exhibits the best performance.

2. **Reliance on a single random split:** All results come from our initial 70/20/10 subject-wise split. A different seed or a different split method could easily reorder model results. 

3. **Modest accuracy on the best models:** An average balanced accuracy of 70% on RQ1 and 50% on RQ2 is not deployable, and accuracy varies from subject to subject. 

4. **Only one task was tested:** While by design, the study's specificity to the n-back experiment leads to a narrow scope on working memory. Other working memory tasks have not been tested on a machine learning pipeline, so we cannot conclusively state that all working memory demand is classifiable. 

5. **The Yedukondalu reproduction is not exact:** While the evaluation results are revealing for the pipelines accuracy on this classification task, the parent study was created and tuned for the MAT and STEW datasets, which exhibit different necessary parameters that the authors were designing the study for.

6. **R-LMD findings are not explored:** The exploratory data analysis revealed that R-LMD may not add sufficient signal for the computing cost it requires, but this was not tested on downstream models.

# Conclusion and Future Work

The results of the final classifier training and testing reveal the answers to our research questions. First, it is clear that n=0 and n=2 can readily be classified by classical machine learning models, and using our relation of n level to working memory, we can conclude that this facet of working memory can be classified. Second, while models did outperform chance when classifying adjacent n levels, they were considerably less accurate. This underperformance was caused mainly by a lack of consistent band power patterns between n-levels, while the binary classification of RQ1 benefitted from the overall patterns present in band power from the lowest to the highest n levels. 

Our results also call into question the generalizability of the parent study's proposed pipeline, which, after correction for data leakage, heavily underperformed on validation data compared to the performance of other models. We attribute this underperformance to heavy feature optimizations within the original pipeline, but our conclusion is limited due to their study's scope being on different data. 

Future work involves investigating facets of this study and developing robust solutions to limitations prevalent in this study. 

1. **Does R-LMD actually work?:** The exploratory data analysis in this study revealed that when applied to these particular datasets, R-LMD tends to introduce no new signal to the classifier's input for a heavy computing cost. Further analysis would test this behavior among different datasets with different filtering scopes, and would A/B test downstream models with and without R-LMD features to check performance differences. 

2. **More robust cross-validation:** This study only examined data through the lens of a single 70/20/10 upstream split, which left little validation data to be used for model selection. Using nested subject-wise CV over all 55 subjects would improve model selection without changing this overall split.

3. **Improving the scope of RQ2:** Instead of comparing overall results of the binary classification to the individual results of adjacent classification, individual results of each should be considered (Comparing Shin n=0, n=3 to Shin 0, 2, 3 would be a fairer comparison than the current implementation).

4. **Alternate dataset selection:** The data selection of this study optimized for volume of n-back experiments, but alternate data could contain multitasking, and in some cases simultaneous multitasking with working memory. Proving model performance on such data would translate readily to proving model performance on actual working memory load variance. 

5. **Alternate join methods:** We used a feature-based join on the disparate datasets due to a lack of shared subjects between them. In conjucntion with the use of alternate data, a subject based join could be completed, which increases trial fidelity per subject and potentially introduces per-subject behavior patterns on different tasks. This would restructure the study into an aggregated set of case studies into detailed subjects. 

6. **Reinforcement Learning:** Instead of training classifiers to distinguish between target n levels, we train an RL model to modify different EEG variables to alter the value of n. This leads to an interesting form of feature extraction: if an RL model learns that a certain EEG signal matters the most to maximizing or minimizing n, that gives us insights into what signals to look for in subsequent trials.
